passage:
Imran, you remember when I stopped coming to the Friday dinners? That was the Sagar year.
Sagar and I met at the library union. He's from a Dalit family; mine is the kind that still asks surnames at weddings. We were friends for two years before we were anything more.
When my mother found out, she didn't shout. She cried, which was worse. My uncle shouted instead. He said a daughter like me had "finished the family."
I wanted to win. I had speeches ready. But Sagar said, "Don't make them choose between you and their pride tonight. Just don't hide me." So I didn't. I brought him to my cousin's birthday. I talked about him at dinner like he was normal, because he is.
It took eighteen months. My mother came to his sister's wedding last winter. My uncle still doesn't speak to me. I'm Nandini, and I'm still standing by him.

qa.q: How long were Nandini and Sagar friends before they were anything more?
qa.a: They were friends for two years before they were anything more.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when her mother cried?
qa.a: Nandini felt guilty and hurt, finding her mother's tears worse than shouting, while also feeling angry and wanting to win the argument.

qa.q: What was the wiser choice Nandini made, and why did it help?
qa.a: Instead of trying to win in one fight, she stopped hiding Sagar and slowly included him in family life, which gave her mother time to change.

qa.q: How might Sagar see the family's reaction?
qa.a: Sagar probably feels hurt by the uncle's anger, but patient, which is why he asks Nandini not to force a choice and just not to hide him.

grounding: A young adult in a cross-caste relationship faces family anger and chooses patience, honesty and standing by her partner over winning in one go.

Sunday. Jaya brought her best friend Pallavi home for lunch for the first time. Jaya's grandmother asked Pallavi her surname, then quietly set out a different steel plate for her. Pallavi noticed. So did Jaya, whose face burned.
Wednesday. Jaya almost called her grandmother to shout. Instead she called Pallavi. "I'm so sorry. I should have said something at the table." Pallavi said, "You don't have to fight her for me. Just don't let me eat alone next time."
The next Sunday. Pallavi came again. When the separate plate appeared, Jaya took it, put her own food on it, and gave Pallavi the family plate. She said calmly, "Dadi, Pallavi is my sister in all but blood." Her grandmother's lips tightened. But later, she offered Pallavi a second helping of kheer.

qa.q: What did Jaya's grandmother set out for Pallavi?
qa.a: She set out a different steel plate for her.

qa.q: How did Jaya feel when she saw the separate plate?
qa.a: Jaya felt ashamed and angry, her face burning, and later guilty for not speaking at the table.

qa.q: Why was Jaya's quiet act on the second Sunday wiser than shouting?
qa.a: She stood by Pallavi without a scene, taking the separate plate herself and speaking calmly, which let her grandmother save face and slowly soften.

qa.q: How might Pallavi have felt at the first lunch?
qa.a: Pallavi probably felt hurt and unwelcome, noticing the different plate but staying silent.

grounding: Across several days, a young adult stands by a friend from another caste against a relative's prejudice, choosing patience and honesty over winning at once.

Eshaan, beta, you think your old Manoj Chacha has always been this calm? No. Let me tell you about Ramesh.
I was twenty-four, working at the sugar mill. Ramesh sat at the next machine. He was from a caste my father would not let into our kitchen. We became friends anyway, over tea and cricket scores.
One day I invited him to my sister's engagement. My father heard and said, "If he comes, I won't." I was so angry I nearly packed my bag and left home.
Instead, I went to Ramesh and told him the truth. He said, "Don't break your family for me. Just don't pretend I'm not your friend." So I went to the engagement, and the next day I went to Ramesh's house for lunch, openly. My father saw. He said nothing for months.
Years later, when my father fell ill, it was Ramesh who drove him to the hospital.

qa.q: Where did Manoj work at twenty-four?
qa.a: He worked at the sugar mill.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when his father said he wouldn't come?
qa.a: Manoj felt so angry that he nearly packed his bag and left home.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Manoj's story?
qa.a: Manoj told Ramesh the truth and, instead of breaking with his family, openly visited Ramesh the next day, standing by his friend while giving his father time.

qa.q: How might Manoj's father have felt when Ramesh drove him to the hospital?
qa.a: He may have felt humbled and grateful, seeing that the man he once refused was a true friend to the family.

grounding: An elder recalls a close friendship across caste, family anger, and how patience and openly standing by the friend mattered more than winning.

passage:
Darshan, come, eat this sewaiyan while I tell you why I make it every Eid, though our family never kept Eid.
I was nine. We lived in a chawl in Byculla, eleven families sharing one long balcony. On Eid morning, Rashida Aunty from the corner room sent over a bowl of sewaiyan. My mother said, "Take something back. Don't return a bowl empty."
So I carried our Diwali ladoos, the last six, to their door. Rashida Aunty hugged me, and her son pulled me in to eat with them on the floor. I remember thinking our balcony was one big house.
Years later, a man at my office said something ugly about "those people." I didn't believe him for a second. I'd eaten from their plates.
That's why, Darshan. Your Damini Nani remembers.

qa.q: How many families shared the long balcony?
qa.a: Eleven families shared one long balcony.

qa.q: How did young Damini feel eating on the floor with Rashida Aunty's family?
qa.a: She felt happy, welcomed and part of something bigger, like the whole balcony was one big house.

qa.q: What was the turning point inside Damini's story?
qa.a: When she carried the ladoos back and was pulled in to eat, the friendship became so real that later prejudice at her office meant nothing to her.

qa.q: How might Rashida Aunty have felt when Damini brought the ladoos?
qa.a: Rashida Aunty was likely touched and happy, which is why she hugged Damini.

grounding: An elder recalls sharing festival sweets with neighbours as a child, feeling part of something bigger, which later made prejudice impossible to believe.

The power went out across the colony on Diwali night, just as Kiran, ten, was about to carry the plate of kaju barfi downstairs to Dilnaz Aunty.
"Wait for the light," Mummy said.
"But Aunty sent us sheer khurma on Eid, and she'll think we forgot."
Mummy sighed and handed her a torch. Kiran went down the dark stairs slowly, holding the plate level with both hands.
Dilnaz Aunty opened the door holding a candle. "Kiran! In this dark?"
"Happy Diwali, Aunty."
Dilnaz Aunty's children crowded round. They lit a candle on the plate and ate the barfi right there on the doorstep, and someone started singing a film song. Kiran climbed back up grinning, the torch swinging.

qa.a: Dilnaz Aunty had sent sheer khurma on Eid.

qa.q: Why did Kiran insist on going in the dark?
qa.a: Kiran was worried that Dilnaz Aunty would think they forgot, and felt it mattered to return the kindness from Eid.

On Christmas Eve, Damini, eight, helped her mother cut plum cake into squares and wrap them in paper napkins. "Who are these for?"
"For the building. Everyone."
Damini carried the tray from flat to flat. The Sharmas gave her a laddu back. Akash's family on the second floor gave her a spoon of kheer, right there at the door. Akash, seven, followed her upstairs to help carry the tray.
At the top floor, old Mr. Bhatia, who lived alone, opened the door slowly. He looked at the cake a long time. "Nobody brings me anything," he said.
Damini gave him two pieces.
Walking down, Akash said, "Next Diwali, we'll do this with our sweets." Damini nodded. The whole building smelled of cake and cardamom.

Dear Jeevan,
You asked how the new school in Leicester is. Mostly okay, even as the only Indian boy in my year. But something happened I want to tell someone.
In RE class, a boy asked if I "worship cows," and made mooing noises. Half the class laughed. Another said Hindus "have a million gods, how do you even keep track?" I went hot all over. I wanted to shout and I wanted to disappear, both at once. I said nothing.
Then my friend Maya said, loudly, "That's not funny. Stop." And Mr. Carter paused the lesson. He said, "That's a stereotype, and it's wrong. Raghav, would you like to share anything? You don't have to." I shook my head. He said he'd talk to the boys after class, and he did.
I felt better, but still a bit sick.
Write back soon,
Raghav

qa.a: Raghav's new school is in Leicester.

qa.q: How did Raghav feel when the class laughed?
qa.a: Raghav went hot all over, feeling angry and ashamed, wanting both to shout and to disappear.

qa.q: How did Maya and Mr. Carter protect Raghav?
qa.a: Maya spoke up loudly, and Mr. Carter paused the lesson, named it as a false stereotype, offered Raghav a choice to speak, and talked to the boys after class.

qa.a: Raghav might keep feeling silenced and ashamed, and the boys might think such jokes were acceptable.

grounding: A teenager hears jokes about his religion in class, feels angry and ashamed, and a friend and teacher protect him by naming the stereotype as false.

Mehak, thanks for having me on. You asked what it's like being Christian in my town. Mostly fine. But I'll tell you about Class 10.
A rumour went round that Christians "pay people to convert." One boy asked, loudly, "So how much did your family get?" People laughed. I laughed too, which I hate now. Then I went home and didn't eat.
The next day, my friend Ruksana stood up in the canteen and said, "Devika's family has been Christian for five generations. She's my friend, and that rumour is rubbish." Our teacher, Mrs. Pillai, heard it and took the whole class through what stereotypes do. She said clearly the rumour was false.
I stopped laughing along after that. That's what I'd tell teenagers now: find the one friend and the one adult. It was the two of them that protected me. I'm Devika, by the way, if anyone's listening.

qa.q: How long has Devika's family been Christian?
qa.a: Devika's family has been Christian for five generations.

qa.q: Why did Devika laugh along and then not eat?
qa.a: Devika laughed to hide shame and hurt, and then felt so upset at home that she didn't eat.

qa.q: What made the difference for Devika?
qa.a: Ruksana spoke up publicly and Mrs. Pillai named the rumour as a false stereotype in front of the class, giving real protection.

qa.a: Ruksana may have felt nervous but determined, angry at the rumour and protective of Devika.

grounding: A teenager hears a false rumour about her faith, feels ashamed and silenced, and is protected by a friend and a teacher who name it as false.

Board exams were four days away, and Afreen, sixteen, couldn't concentrate. Her best friend Manjula hadn't replied to a single message since the weekend.
There had been violence in a town two hours away, and it was on every channel. On Monday, Manjula sat at a different desk. On Tuesday, she walked home with other girls.
Afreen's first thought was, She thinks I'm one of "them." Her second was, Maybe her family told her to stay away.
With no time to waste, she wrote a note and slipped it into Manjula's bag: "I miss you. Did something happen? I'm not angry. I just want to know."
On Wednesday, Manjula found her at the gate. Her eyes were red. "My Papa said to keep away for a while. I didn't know how to tell you."
"It's not your fault," Afreen said. "Study with me after the exams? When it's calmer?"
Manjula nodded and squeezed her hand.

qa.q: What did Afreen slip into Manjula's bag?
qa.a: She slipped in a note: "I miss you. Did something happen? I'm not angry. I just want to know."

qa.q: What was Afreen worried about when Manjula pulled away?
qa.a: Afreen was hurt and afraid that Manjula now saw her as one of "them" because of the violence, or had been told to stay away.

After the clash in the city made the headlines, Varun Mathew stopped coming to the colony basketball court. Sunaina, seventeen, waited for him three evenings in a row.
She finally knocked at his flat. His mother answered, polite but guarded. Varun came to the door and didn't step out.
"Did I do something?" Sunaina asked.
Varun looked at his feet. "People in our church are scared. My mother thinks we should keep to ourselves for a bit. Your uncle posted something online."
Sunaina's face went hot. She'd seen that post and said nothing.
"That's not what I think," she said. "And you're not responsible for what anyone else did either. I'm sorry I didn't say so sooner."
Varun's shoulders dropped a little. "Court tomorrow?"
"Six o'clock. I'll bring the ball."

Last December, Jomon invited me to midnight mass at his church in Kochi. I'm Pradeep, and I'd never been inside a church in my life. I was curious, and a little nervous about doing something wrong.
Before we went, I asked him, "What should I not do?" He laughed and said, "Don't take communion, just sit, and stand when we stand." I wore a plain shirt and left my phone on silent.
Inside, the candles and the choir were beautiful. I didn't know the words, so I just listened. At one point an old lady handed me her hymn book, open to the right page. I thanked her with a nod.
Afterwards, over plum cake at Jomon's house, I asked his father about why the carols mattered to him. He talked for an hour.
I'm still who I was. But I understand Jomon a little more.

Faculty note, comparative religion elective, field visit, Saturday.
We visited the Buddhist vihara where Kalyani's family has been going for years. Kalyani offered to guide the class.
Dhruv, 20, stayed close to her the whole visit. Before entering, he asked her quietly whether he should remove his shoes and whether he could sit on the mats. When the monks began chanting, he sat still with his hands folded, as Kalyani did, and did not take photos, though several others did.
Afterwards he asked a monk, politely, what the chant meant and why people bowed three times. He listened without arguing. On the bus back, he told Kalyani, "I don't think I'd ever follow it, but I get why it matters to you." She smiled.
Next step: I will ask Dhruv and Kalyani to lead a short discussion next week on visiting another faith's space respectfully.

passage:
Sunday night
Went with Swati and her family to the Jain temple for Paryushan today. First time.
I was nervous. Swati had told me: no leather, no food inside, don't touch the idols, wash hands and feet first. I borrowed cloth shoes from my brother and kept my wallet at home.
Inside, it was quiet and white and smelled of sandalwood. Swati's grandmother was doing a long prayer, and I just sat at the back. I didn't understand the words, but I understood the stillness.
Afterwards I asked Swati's grandmother why they say sorry to everyone during Paryushan. She said, "Michchhami Dukkadam. We ask forgiveness for any hurt, even ones we don't know we caused." I found that beautiful.
I'm not becoming Jain. Swati knows that, and her family didn't ask me to. I just wanted to understand her better, and I think I do.
Vikas

qa.a: Swati said no leather, no food inside, don't touch the idols, and wash hands and feet first.

qa.q: How did Vikas feel sitting at the back during the prayer?
qa.a: Vikas felt nervous at first and then calm and moved by the stillness, even without understanding the words.

qa.q: Why is Vikas's approach a good model for visiting another faith?
qa.a: Vikas prepared by learning the rules, stayed respectful and quiet, and asked a genuine question afterwards, all without any aim of changing belief.
